```{r setup}
library(pollinatoR)
```

## The design

A three-arm trial puts three pollination treatments side by side: plants
*excluded* from insects (caged or bagged), plants left *open* to whatever
pollinators visit, and plants *supplemented* by hand with extra pollen. The
three arms answer two different questions.

* The deficit (E1) compares supplemented with open plants. It asks how much
  yield was left on the table by the pollination the crop actually received.
* The dependence (E2) compares excluded plants with a reference arm. It asks
  how much yield is owed to pollinators. The reference is usually the open arm;
  in a three-arm trial it can also be the supplemented arm, which gives the
  dependence under full pollination.

This vignette simulates a small randomised complete block trial: eight blocks,
each holding all three arms, with six plants per arm in each block. The
response is pod count per plant.

```{r data}
set.seed(2024)
n_block <- 8L
n_plant <- 6L
arms <- c("Bagged", "Open", "Hand")
trial <- expand.grid(
  plant = seq_len(n_plant),
  trt = arms,
  block = sprintf("B%d", seq_len(n_block)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
block_effect <- rnorm(n_block, 0, 0.15)
arm_mean <- c(Bagged = 40, Open = 60, Hand = 70)
names(block_effect) <- sprintf("B%d", seq_len(n_block))
mu <- arm_mean[trial$trt] * exp(block_effect[trial$block])
trial$pods <- rnbinom(nrow(trial), mu = mu, size = 30)
head(trial)
```

The planted arm means are 40, 60 and 70 pods. On these values the dependence on
the open arm is a loss share of $1 - 40/60 = 0.33$, and the deficit is a loss
share of $1 - 60/70 = 0.14$.

## Data, design and estimand

The data step names the columns; the design step maps each treatment level to
its role and fixes the layout. In a randomised complete block layout the block
carries a random intercept.

```{r declare}
pd <- pollin_data(trial, response = "pods", treatment = "trt", unit = "block")
ds <- pollin_design(
  pd,
  arms = c(excluded = "Bagged", open = "Open", supplemented = "Hand"),
  layout = "rcbd"
)
ds
```

The estimand step names the contrast, the scale and the basis. Neither the scale
nor the basis has a default.

```{r estimand}
deficit <- pollin_estimand(ds, family = "deficit", scale = "ratio", basis = "loss")
deficit
knitr::kable(pollin_assumptions(deficit))
```

The assumption table is the part of the analysis the data cannot check. For the
deficit, the key one is that hand supplementation adds pollen and nothing else;
for the dependence, it is that the bag or cage excludes insects without changing
the plant's microclimate.

## Loss share or gain

The same pair of arm means can be reported in two ways. The loss share is the
fraction of the higher arm's yield that is lost without the contrast,
$1 - \mathrm{low}/\mathrm{high}$. The gain is the increase over the lower arm,
$\mathrm{high}/\mathrm{low} - 1$. For the dependence planted here, the loss share
is 0.33 and the gain is 0.50. The two answer different questions: the loss
share is the part of current yield that pollinators supply, which is what a
valuation of their service needs, and the gain is how much a crop without them
would rise if they returned. Reporting a gain where a loss share was meant
overstates the value by a factor of $1/(1 - D)$.

`basis` is therefore stated every time, and printed on every result.

```{r basis}
fit_effect <- function(design, family, scale, basis) {
  est <- pollin_estimand(design, family = family, scale = scale, basis = basis)
  pollin_effects(pollin_fit(est))$table
}
dep_loss <- fit_effect(ds, "dependence", "ratio", "loss")
dep_gain <- fit_effect(ds, "dependence", "ratio", "gain")
rbind(dep_loss, dep_gain)[, c("contrast", "basis", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")]
```

The interval for a ratio-type scale is a delta interval for the log ratio of
the averaged predictions, transformed to the scale, so a loss share stays below
one.

Both intervals cover the planted values. A parametric bootstrap gives a
second interval: responses are simulated from the fitted model, the model is
refitted to each simulated set, and the interval is taken from the percentiles
of the refitted estimates. Use several hundred refits in an analysis; the 100
here keep the example quick.

```{r bootstrap}
est_dep <- pollin_estimand(ds, family = "dependence", scale = "ratio", basis = "loss")
pollin_effects(pollin_fit(est_dep), interval = "bootstrap", n_boot = 100L, seed = 1L)
```

## Both estimands on several scales

The estimate is always formed from the model's expected response in each arm,
averaged over the trial's plants: a ratio of averaged predictions, never an
average of plant-level ratios. The scale only changes how that pair of
expected values is reported.

```{r scales}
grid <- expand.grid(
  family = c("deficit", "dependence"),
  scale = c("difference", "ratio", "rii", "lnrr"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) {
  fit_effect(ds, grid$family[i], grid$scale[i], basis = "loss")
})
effects <- do.call(rbind, rows)
effects[, c("family", "contrast", "scale", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")]
```

The RII and the loss share are linked by $\mathrm{RII} = D/(2 - D)$, and the log
response ratio is $\log(\mathrm{high}/\mathrm{low})$, so the three ratio-type
rows for each family carry the same information on different scales. All rows
here use `basis = "loss"`; the basis changes the value only on the ratio scale.
The difference scale is in pods per plant.

## Dependence against the supplemented arm

With `reference = "supplemented"` the dependence compares excluded plants with
hand-pollinated ones. This is the dependence under full pollination, an upper
reference for the crop's need for pollinators, while the open reference gives
the dependence realised in the field.

```{r reference}
ds_sup <- pollin_design(
  pd,
  arms = c(excluded = "Bagged", open = "Open", supplemented = "Hand"),
  layout = "rcbd",
  reference = "supplemented"
)
est_sup <- pollin_estimand(ds_sup, "dependence", scale = "ratio", basis = "loss")
pollin_effects(pollin_fit(est_sup))
```

## A sham arm

A bag or cage does more than keep insects out: it shades the plant and changes
the air around it. The dependence above includes any such effect, because the
excluded plants carry the device and the open plants do not. A sham arm
carries the same device with its sides open, so insects reach the plant. The
trial below swaps the hand-pollinated arm for a sham, and the device raises
pod count by 10% whether or not insects visit.

```{r sham-data}
set.seed(2025)
sham_trial <- expand.grid(
  plant = seq_len(n_plant),
  trt = c("Bagged", "Open", "Sham"),
  block = sprintf("B%d", seq_len(n_block)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
sham_mean <- c(Bagged = 44, Open = 60, Sham = 66)
mu <- sham_mean[sham_trial$trt] * exp(block_effect[sham_trial$block])
sham_trial$pods <- rnbinom(nrow(sham_trial), mu = mu, size = 30)
pd_sham <- pollin_data(sham_trial, "pods", "trt", unit = "block")
sham_arms <- c(excluded = "Bagged", open = "Open", sham = "Sham")
```

The `cage` family estimates the device's own effect, the sham against the
open arm. On the ratio scale it is the factor by which the device multiplies
pod count, planted at 1.1.

```{r cage}
ds_sham <- pollin_design(pd_sham, sham_arms, layout = "rcbd")
pollin_effects(pollin_fit(pollin_estimand(ds_sham, "cage", "ratio")))
```

Read against the sham, the dependence compares two bagged arms that differ
only in whether insects get in. It is net of the device, planted at
$1 - 44/66 = 0.33$, where the contrast with the open arm gives
$1 - 44/60 = 0.27$.

```{r sham-reference}
ds_net <- pollin_design(pd_sham, sham_arms, layout = "rcbd", reference = "sham")
est_net <- pollin_estimand(ds_net, "dependence", scale = "ratio", basis = "loss")
pollin_effects(pollin_fit(est_net))
```

This reading assumes the device multiplies pod count by the same factor with
and without insects, and `pollin_assumptions(est_net)` states it. A trial
with only the sham and the excluded arm reads the dependence the same way but
cannot estimate the device's effect. Without a sham arm, `pollin_bound()`
bounds the share over a range of device effects (*Identification in a field
study*).

## A guard on plant-level ratios

A common shortcut computes the RII or the dependence ratio for each block (or
each plant) and averages them. The mean of bounded unit-level ratios is not the
ratio of the expected values, and `pollin_guard_bounded()` refuses it unless
asked.

```{r guard-refuse}
try(pollin_guard_bounded(ds, index = "dependence"))
```

When the average is wanted for comparison with earlier work, `allow = TRUE`
returns it with the statement attached and the ratio of the arm means beside it.

```{r guard-allow}
pollin_guard_bounded(ds, index = "dependence", allow = TRUE)
```

Here the block means differ only a little, so the two numbers are close. They
separate when units differ widely in yield, which is common across sites and
varieties.
